title: Scientists use 'big puffy atoms' to unlock a new path for quantum computing
excerpt: Researchers at the University of Tennessee (UT) have developed a protocol to test quantum entanglement in Motzkin spin chains, which could help advance quantum computing in the future.
content:
Researchers at the University of Tennessee (UT) Knoxville and UT Chattanooga teamed up to develop a practical way to test quantum entanglement. Working with Motzkin spin chains, the researchers devised a blueprint to test this unusual entanglement, which could help develop quantum computers in the future.

Quantum physics is something that even Albert Einstein found 'spooky' at times and difficult to explain. Even though we have a pretty good idea of how bodies react in the physical world, at the quantum level, the rules of standard physics do not seem to apply at all.  

The little bit of quantum physics what we understand is helping us build futuristic technologies like quantum computing and sensing. But researchers Adrian Del Maestro, a professor in the Department of Physics and Astronomy at UT Knoxville, and Rick Mukherjee, an associate professor of physics at UT Chattanooga, collaborated to turn a mathematical oddity concerning Motzkin spin chains into reality.

Why are Motzkin spin chains unique? 

Motzkin spin chains are one-dimensional quantum spin models whose ground state is a superposition of Motzkin walks or lattice paths that start and end at height zero, without dipping below. They serve as a bridge between quantum information and condensed matter physics and include two elements that are extremely important for quantum computing: entanglement and superposition.

In his work, Stephen Hawking found out that even black holes follow the area law. I.e., their entropy grows proportionally to their surface area. Interestingly, Motzkin spin chains do not follow this law.

Since each site contains two quantum states, Motzkin spin chains are difficult to simulate on classical computers. Del Maestro's lab has long been working to realize these spin chains in the lab but has not succeeded. When he mentioned it to Mukherjee, the latter said it could be made possible using Rydberg atoms. 

How Rydberg atoms can help 

Mukherjee refers to Rydberg atoms as 'big puffy atoms' that can be excited into high-energy states. They can be moved around using lasers and light patterns, and knowing what constraints can be used where helps physicists turn the right knobs to get these atoms in their experiments.

Working with these atoms, Del Maestro's group succeeded in tuning them in and out of a structure that showed entanglement, much like in a Motzkin state. Del Maestro's group identified the fingerprint for this state, while Mukherjee's expertise in knowing which knobs to turn to get it brought together a new protocol to reach this entangled state for something that is a mathematical oddity.

The teams are still away from realizing this experimentally inside a laboratory but are keen to collaborate with researchers who regularly work with Rydberg atoms to attempt this in the lab. 

"Quantum science doesn't respect the traditional boundaries of physics," said Mukherjee in a press release. "The questions condensed matter physicists have asked for decades, about entanglement, exotic phases and how many particles behave collectively, are now questions we can test directly by building quantum systems atom by atom."

Del Maestro admits this may be a small step toward understanding quantum physics but hopes the experiments lead to something very interesting in the future.

The research findings were published in the journal Physical Review Letters.
